Part A: Principles, Roles & Assessment Process

Assessing Fitness to Drive (Austroads/NTC, 2022) — Australian national medical standards for driver licensing

Source document: Assessing Fitness to Drive 2022, joint publication of Austroads and the National Transport Commission (NTC). First published in current form 2003; previous edition 2016. Approved by Commonwealth, state and territory transport ministers. Endorsed by: Australasian Faculty of Occupational and Environmental Medicine, Australasian Faculty of Rehabilitation Medicine, Australasian Sleep Association, Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists, Australian College of Rural and Remote Medicine, Australian Diabetes Society, Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand, Occupational Therapy Australia, Royal Australian College of Physicians. Accepted clinical resource of the RACGP.

This publication replaces all previous editions: Assessing Fitness to Drive 2001, 2003, 2012, 2016 (and 2017 amendment) and Medical Examinations for Commercial Vehicle Drivers 1997.

Legal disclaimer: compiled with reasonable care based on expert medical opinion and literature; neither Austroads nor the authors accept responsibility for consequences of application. Health professionals must keep up to date with healthcare/technology changes and legal changes affecting their responsibilities. Ethical/legal concerns → medical defence organisation or legal advisor. Other queries → relevant driver licensing authority (DLA).

Context (Foreword): In 2020, 1,106 people were killed on Australian roads; tens of thousands hospitalised with serious injuries. Annual economic cost of road crashes in Australia ≈ $30 billion. Draft guidelines were released for public consultation in May 2021.

1. About this publication

1.1. Purpose

Driving is a complex task involving perception, appropriate judgement, adequate response time and appropriate physical capability. Medical conditions, disabilities and treatments may influence these prerequisites; impairment may adversely affect driving ability, possibly causing a crash resulting in death or injury.

Primary purpose — to increase road safety in Australia by assisting health professionals to:

  • assess fitness to drive of patients consistently and appropriately based on current medical evidence
  • promote responsible patient behaviour with regard to medical fitness
  • conduct medical examinations for licensing as required by state/territory DLAs
  • provide information to inform decisions on conditional licences
  • recognise the extent and limits of their professional and legal obligations regarding reporting fitness to drive.

Also aims to guide DLAs in licensing decisions. The publication:

  • outlines clear medical requirements for driver capability based on evidence and expert opinion
  • clearly differentiates national minimum standards (approved by the Infrastructure and Transport Ministers’ Meeting) for commercial vs private vehicle drivers
  • provides general guidelines for managing patients re: fitness to drive
  • outlines legal obligations of health professionals, DLAs and drivers
  • provides a reporting template to guide reporting to the DLA if required
  • provides links to supporting/substantiating information.

Routine use ensures consistent assessment and may minimise the health professional’s medico-legal exposure if a patient is later involved in a crash or disputes a licensing decision.

1.2. Target audience

Intended for any health professional involved in assessing fitness to drive or supporting fitness-to-drive decisions, including:

  • medical practitioners (GPs and specialists)
  • optometrists
  • orthoptists
  • occupational therapists
  • psychologists
  • physiotherapists
  • diabetes educators
  • nurse practitioners and primary health care nurses
  • case workers.

Also the primary source of requirements for DLAs making determinations about medical fitness to hold a licence.

1.3. Scope

1.3.1. Medical fitness for driver licensing. Designed principally to guide/support health professional assessments for licensing purposes. Should be used when:

  1. Treating any patient who holds a driver licence whose condition may affect their ability to drive safely. Most adults drive; a health professional should routinely consider impact of a patient’s condition on safe driving. Be aware of patient’s occupation, licence category (commercial, passenger vehicle) and driving requirements (e.g. shift work).
  2. Undertaking an examination at the request of a DLA or industry accreditation body. Health professionals may be asked to examine a driver for reasons including:
    • initial licensing of some vehicle classes (e.g. multiple combination heavy vehicles)
    • as a requirement for a conditional licence
    • assessing a person whose driving the DLA believes may be unsafe (“for cause” examinations)
    • licence renewal of an older driver (in certain states/territories)
    • licensing/accreditation of certain commercial vehicle drivers (e.g. public passenger vehicle drivers)
    • as a requirement for Basic or Advanced Fatigue Management under the National Heavy Vehicle Accreditation Scheme (see www.nhvr.gov.au).

Focuses on long-term health- and disability-related conditions and functional effects impacting driving. Sets minimum medical requirements for unconditional and conditional licences forming the medical basis for DLA decisions. Two sets of standards: private vehicle driver standards and commercial vehicle driver standards.

Standards apply to drivers within the ambit of ordinary road laws. Drivers with special exemptions (e.g. emergency service vehicle drivers) should have a risk assessment and an appropriate medical standard applied by their employer; at minimum, assessed to the commercial vehicle standard.

1.3.2. Short-term fitness to drive. Does not attempt to address the full range of conditions affecting fitness to drive in the short term (see section 2.2.3 Temporary conditions). Non-driving period for short-term conditions generally determined by the treating health professional based on assessment of the condition and potential risks.

1.3.3. Fitness for duty. The medical standards relate only to driving — cannot be assumed to apply to fitness-for-duty assessments (e.g. checking loads, conversing with passengers, emergency procedures) without first undertaking a task risk assessment identifying the full range of job requirements.

1.4. Content

Presented in three parts:

Part A — general information: principles of assessing fitness to drive; specific considerations (multiple conditions/age-related change, temporary conditions, progressive disorders and undifferentiated illness, effects of prescription/OTC drugs, role of practical driver assessments and rehabilitation); roles/responsibilities of drivers, licensing authorities and health professionals; which standards to apply (private/commercial); conditional licences; steps involved in assessing fitness to drive.

Part B — chapters on relevant medical systems/diseases. Medical requirements for unconditional and conditional licences summarised in tabulated format differentiating private vs commercial requirements; rationale and general assessment/management guidance in supporting text.

Part C (Appendices) — regulatory requirements for driver assessment per jurisdiction; forms guidance; legislation on reporting; blood alcohol/seatbelt/helmet/interlock legislation; contacts for disabled parking/transport, OT assessments and DLAs.

1.5. Development and evidence base

Evidence underpinning licensing criteria: medical and fitness-to-drive studies, medical guidelines, expert opinion. Reference lists at the end of each chapter.

Key evidence source: Monash University Accident Research Centre report, Influence of chronic illness on crash involvement of motor vehicle drivers: 3rd edition (update of 2nd/2010 edition) — comprehensive review of published studies of private and commercial drivers, examining crash involvement in the context of condition prevalence and quality of evidence.

Sources of potential bias noted in interpreting the evidence:

  • “Healthy driver” effect — drivers with a medical condition may self-restrict or cease driving, reducing crash opportunity and lowering apparent crash risk.
  • Crash definition/incidence often relies on self-report → over/under-reporting.
  • “Medical condition” defined by self-report in some studies → may be inaccurate.
  • “Exposure metric” (km travelled) often uncontrolled, though crucial to crash risk.
  • Small, unrepresentative sample sizes.
  • Control groups not properly matched by age/sex.
  • Commercial drivers rarely considered as a separate cohort.
  • Studies rarely identify whether drivers are treated/untreated (e.g. corrected vision, hearing aids).
  • Comorbidities may not be adjusted for (e.g. alcohol dependence).

Implication: false-negative results may occur (condition appears to have no/minimal effect on driving safety); professional opinion plus other relevant data must be considered alongside the literature. The review excluded technical reports, conference presentations/abstracts, case studies, coroner reports/studies, cohort studies without a control group, and reviews of consensus-based standards.

Definition of “crash” (for this publication): a collision between two or more vehicles, or any other accident/incident involving a vehicle in which a person or animal is killed or injured, or property is damaged.

Health professionals should keep up to date with medical knowledge/technology changes and legislation affecting duties.

2. Assessing fitness to drive — general guidance

Aim: balance between (a) minimising driving-related road safety risks posed by the driver’s permanent/long-term injury or illness, and (b) maintaining the driver’s lifestyle and employment-related mobility independence.

Key question: Is there a likelihood the person will be unable to control the vehicle and/or unable to act or react to the driving environment in a safe, consistent and timely manner?

Main considerations in making the assessment:

  • the driving task, including individual driving requirements and mobility needs
  • potential impacts of medical conditions, disabilities and treatments
  • the driver’s functional abilities, including capacity to compensate and need for rehabilitation.

Threshold tolerance is much lower for commercial vehicle drivers, given more time on the road and more severe crash consequences. In borderline cases, health professional may advise conditions under which driving could be performed safely (conditional licence).

2.1. The driving task

Driving is a complex instrumental activity of daily living, characterised by a rapidly repeating cycle:

  1. Information about the vehicle and road environment obtained via visual and auditory senses.
  2. Information operated on by several cognitive processes → decisions about driving.
  3. Decisions put into effect via the musculoskeletal system, acting on vehicle controls (Figure 1: Sensory input → Vehicle-road interaction / Cognitive input → Musculoskeletal actions → loop).

The repeating sequence depends on:

Sensory input: vision; visuospatial perception; hearing; proprioception; kinesthesia.

Motor function: muscle power; coordination.

Cognitive function: attention and concentration; comprehension; memory; insight; judgement; decision making; reaction time; sensation.

Many body systems must be functional for safe, timely execution of driving skills. Demands vary considerably with driver, vehicle, purpose and road environment factors — significant for commercial drivers.

Assessing health professionals should document the individual’s driving requirements and driving history as part of the assessment process.

Box 1. Factors affecting driving — driving occurs within a dynamic system influenced by:

  • driver’s experience, training and attitude
  • driver’s physical, mental and emotional health (e.g. fatigue, substance misuse — illicit, prescription, non-prescription drugs)
  • the road system (signs, other road users, traffic characteristics, road layout)
  • legal requirements (e.g. speed limits, blood alcohol concentration)
  • natural environment (night, weather extremes, glare)
  • vehicle/equipment characteristics (vehicle type, braking performance, maintenance)
  • mental workload/distraction from in-vehicle technologies (GPS, warning/driver assistance systems) and communication systems (hands-free phone/email)
  • personal requirements, trip purpose, destination, appointments, navigation, time pressures
  • passengers, in-vehicle communication/entertainment devices.

For commercial or heavy vehicle drivers, additional factors:

  • business requirements (rosters/shifts, training, contractual demands)
  • work-related multitasking (GPS, job display screens, communication systems)
  • legal requirements (work diaries, licensing procedures)
  • vehicle issues (size, stability, load distribution)
  • passenger requirements/duty of care, occupational violence risk
  • risks of carrying dangerous goods
  • additional vehicle-management skills (turning, braking)
  • endurance/fatigue/vigilance demands of long periods on the road.

2.2. Impact of medical conditions on driving

2.2.1. Assessing medical conditions. Key domains when assessing impact of medical conditions/disabilities:

  • impairment of sensory function (visual acuity/fields; also cutaneous, muscle, joint sensation)
  • impairment of motor function (joint movement, strength, endurance, coordination)
  • impairment of cognition (attention, concentration, memory, problem-solving, thought processing, visuospatial skills, insight, judgement)
  • the risk of sudden incapacity (leading to sudden loss of control of the vehicle).

Conditions with potential for significant impairment and/or sudden incapacity that are the focus of this publication:

  • blackouts
  • cardiovascular conditions
  • diabetes
  • hearing loss and deafness
  • musculoskeletal conditions
  • neurological conditions
  • psychiatric conditions
  • substance misuse/dependency
  • sleep disorders
  • vision problems.

Impairments/impacts may be framed as:

  • Persistent (e.g. visual impairment) vs episodic (e.g. seizure, severe hypoglycaemic event). Persistent impairments assessed via observation/measures of functional capacity; episodic impairment assessed via risk analysis considering probability and consequence of the episode, triggering factors, and whether avoidable.
  • Fluctuating — e.g. capacity of people living with dementia can fluctuate day-to-day and within a 24-hour period; assessor must consider fluctuating capacity’s impact on driving ability.
  • Progressive (e.g. dementia, progressive neurological conditions, end-organ effects of diabetes) or static (permanent disabilities) — has implications for ongoing monitoring. Many people with long-term conditions/disabilities develop coping strategies for safe driving.
  • Medication-introduced — via drugs affecting cognition and reaction time.
  • Resolving with treatment (e.g. following stroke rehabilitation) — implications for reinstating unconditional licences.

2.2.2. Conditions not covered explicitly in this publication. Not all clinical situations/combinations can be defined; professional judgement required. General principles: consider the driving task and potential impact on sensory/motor/cognitive skills; episodic conditions need consideration of recurrence likelihood; a more stringent threshold applies to commercial drivers; an appropriate review period should be advised depending on natural history.

2.2.3. Temporary conditions. Wide range of conditions temporarily affect ability to drive safely (post-surgery recovery, severe migraine, limb injuries) — self-limiting, do not affect licence status; DLA does not need to be informed. Treating health professional should advise on driving safely, including recommended abstinence periods, especially for commercial drivers.

Table 1. Examples of how to manage temporary conditions

Condition and impact on driving Management guidelines
Anaesthesia and sedation — physical/mental capacity may be impaired post-anaesthesia (general, local, sedation); depends on duration of anaesthesia, drugs, surgery performed. Local anaesthesia effect depends on dosage/region. Responsibility of surgeon/dentist and anaesthetist to advise not to drive until recovery compatible with safe driving. Minor procedures under local anaesthesia without sedation (e.g. dental block): driving may be acceptable immediately after. Brief surgery/procedures with short-acting anaesthetic/sedation: fit to drive after a normal night’s sleep. Longer surgery/procedures requiring general anaesthesia or sedation: may not be safe to drive for 24 hours or more.
Deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism — DVT may lead to acute pulmonary embolus; little evidence such an event causes crashes; no licensing standard applies. Private and commercial drivers advised not to drive for at least 2 weeks following a DVT and for 6 weeks following a pulmonary embolism. If long-term anticoagulation prescribed, apply standard for anticoagulant therapy (Part B 2.2.8).
Medications or other treatments — adaptation to new drug regimens or treatments (e.g. radiation therapy, haemodialysis) may require a non-driving period. Non-driving period determined by treating health professional based on requirements of the driving task and impact of medication/treatment on capacity, including responding to emergencies. Practical driver assessment may help.
Post-surgery — driving ability affected to varying degrees depending on location, nature, extent of procedure. Non-driving period determined by treating health professional similarly. Practical driver assessment may help.
Pregnancy — under normal circumstances not a barrier to driving; conditions to consider: fainting/light-headedness, hyperemesis gravidarum, hypertension of pregnancy, post-caesarean section. Caution regarding driving may be required depending on severity of symptoms and expected medication effects. Seatbelts must be worn (Appendix 7).
Temporary or short-term vision impairments — e.g. temporary eye patching, mydriatics/other vision-impairing drugs, eye surgery. Advise not to drive for an appropriate period.

2.2.4. Undifferentiated conditions. A patient may present with symptoms with unclear diagnosis but potential licence implications — period of uncertainty before definitive diagnosis. Each situation assessed individually, considering probability of a serious disease/long-term illness affecting driving, and circumstances of required driving. Patients with symptoms of a serious nature (e.g. chest pains, dizzy spells, blackouts, delusional states) should be advised not to drive until adequately assessed. During this interim period, for private drivers, no formal communication with the DLA is required unless significant risk to public health exists. After diagnosis is firmly established, normal notification procedures apply. For a commercial vehicle driver with symptoms of a potentially serious nature: advise to stop driving and notify the DLA; consider impact on livelihood; investigate as quickly as possible.

2.2.5. Progressive conditions. Diagnoses of progressive conditions (e.g. multiple sclerosis, early dementia) are often made well before there is a need to question ongoing safety to drive — but issues re: likely effects on personal mobility should be raised early. Patient should be advised appropriately, giving as much lead time as possible for lifestyle changes (e.g. adaptation to public transport, motorised mobility device). Occupational therapist assistance may be valuable (Part B 6.1 Dementia).

2.2.6. Congenital conditions, disability and driving. Physical/cognitive implications may include (not limited to):

  • difficulty sustaining concentration or switching attention between multiple driving tasks
  • reduced cognitive/perceptual processing speeds, including reaction times
  • reduced performance in complex situations (e.g. multiple distractions)
  • reduced information processing and judgement
  • difficulty anticipating/responding to other road users
  • difficulty controlling movement
  • reduced joint range of motion and muscle strength.

Many people develop coping strategies. Individual assessment required based on general principles, stability of the disability, and bodily systems underpinning adaptive behaviours. Legal reporting obligations apply (3.2). May trigger need for a medical report and/or occupational therapy driving assessment — an OT driver assessor can advise on aids, vehicle modifications, training strategies. Outcomes may result in a conditional licence (driver condition, e.g. prosthesis must be worn; or vehicle condition, e.g. modifications). If the condition/disability is static, periodic review unlikely required.

Learning to drive: people with a disability can seek to gain a licence, increasingly supported via the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS). Helpful to be trained by an instructor experienced with disabilities. Initial OT assessment (specialised in driver evaluation) may identify functional capacity requirements, need for adaptive devices, vehicle modifications or special techniques.

National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS): provides all Australians under 65 with a permanent/significant disability reasonable and necessary supports, potentially including assistance with medical review process, obtaining licence, medical reports, OT driving assessments, driver training, vehicle modifications (www.ndis.gov.au).

2.2.7. Older drivers and age-related changes. Advanced age alone is not a barrier to safe driving, but age-related physical/mental changes will eventually affect ability. Given the association between health outcomes, mobility and social connectedness, fitness to drive should be proactively managed, aiming to enable continued driving as long as safe.

Crash data: older drivers more likely to crash at intersections and in multi-vehicle crashes; frailty associated with higher risk of injury/death. Safety risks may be mitigated by extensive driving experience and self-modified driving (avoiding peak-hour traffic, poor weather, night driving; slower speeds).

Management approach — encompasses primary, secondary and tertiary prevention:

  • Discussions about mobility and driving: early conversations (before the conversation is only about ceasing driving) focused on maintenance of ability in the context of general health/mobility/ADLs build self-awareness and normalise eventual transition to non-driving. DLAs provide resources to support these conversations.
  • Active observation and screening: routine care should monitor decline in vision, cognition, motor/sensory function. Opportunity to pick up “red flags” — falls, memory problems, confusion, caregiver concerns, sudden change in social circumstances. Annual checks (e.g. Medicare 75 Plus health check) provide screening opportunity.
  • Early intervention: early identification of functional decline → referral for allied health/driver assessment, treatments, driving rehabilitation, vehicle modifications, driving restrictions. Health professional may advise conditions for safe driving (conditional licence); referral to a geriatrician may assist if doubt exists about fitness to drive or remedial strategies.
  • Considering impact of medical conditions: most older adults have ≥1 chronic condition. Most common: cardiovascular disease, stroke, Parkinson’s disease, sleep disorders, cataracts, glaucoma, musculoskeletal impairments including arthritis, depression, dementia, diabetes. Overall impact of multiple conditions must be considered (2.2.8). A new diagnosis/change in condition or an acute medical event, or addition of a new medication/treatment, is a trigger to revisit driving. Older adults often take multiple medications → increased crash risk; counselling should address safety concerns including age-associated changed drug metabolism (2.2.9).
  • Transition to alternative transport: when functioning is no longer compatible with safe driving, support in relinquishing licence and seeking alternatives is needed. Ongoing monitoring of health/social consequences and compliance with advice not to drive. Caregivers play an important role encouraging cessation and helping find alternatives.

Assessing older drivers — three main functional areas:

  • Vision: acuity, visual fields, contrast sensitivity may decline; cataracts, glaucoma, macular degeneration more common. Gradual onset may go unnoticed. Regular eye checks facilitate early detection. Difficulty at night with glare may be an early sign. Restrictions such as no-night-driving can help maintain safe driving; cataract removal can effectively restore vision.
  • Cognition: memory, working memory, visuospatial skills, attention, executive functioning, insight can decline — affects processing/responding to the complex road environment; can vary day to day. Dementia is a particular concern as older adults often lack insight into deficits (Part B 6.1 Dementia).
  • Motor and somatosensory function: decline in muscle strength/endurance, reduced flexibility/range of motion/joint stability; musculoskeletal conditions (e.g. arthritis) more prevalent; proprioception may be an issue. May cause difficulty getting in/out of car, seatbelt, ignition key, mirrors, seats, steering, reversing, foot pedals. Adaptive equipment available; rehabilitative therapies may improve functioning/endurance.

More information: RACGP’s Guidelines for preventative activities in general practice (“Red Book”) and Aged care clinical guide (“Silver Book”).

2.2.8. Multiple medical conditions. Where a driver has multiple conditions or a condition affecting multiple body systems, there may be an additive or compounding detrimental effect on driving abilities. Examples:

  • congenital disabilities (cerebral palsy, spina bifida, various syndromes)
  • multiple trauma causing orthopaedic and neurological injuries plus psychiatric sequelae
  • multi-system diseases (diabetes, connective tissue disease, multiple sclerosis, systemic lupus erythematosus)
  • dual diagnoses involving psychiatric illness and drug/alcohol addiction
  • ageing-related changes in motor, cognitive and sensory abilities together with degenerative disease
  • chronic pain.

Clinical judgement is needed to integrate the effects of all conditions — it is insufficient to apply the standards for each condition separately, because several minor impairments together may make risks unacceptable even if each alone would not. Where conditions are progressive, it may be important to reduce driving exposure and ensure ongoing monitoring; conditional licences that limit the driver (no night driving) or vehicle (automatic transmission only) are an option. Periodic review requirements can be included as licence recommendations.

Periodic reviews are important for conditions likely to be associated with future reductions in insight/self-regulation. If lack of insight may become an issue, advise the patient to report to the DLA. Where lack of insight already appears to impair self-assessment/judgement, public safety interests should prevail — the health professional should report directly to the DLA and, if appropriate, seek support of the patient’s family members.

2.2.9. Drugs and driving. Any CNS-acting drug has potential to adversely affect driving skills. CNS depressants may reduce vigilance, increase reaction times, impair decision making similarly to alcohol. Drugs affecting behaviour may exaggerate adverse behavioural traits and introduce risk-taking behaviours.

Considerations when assessing/managing medication relevant to fitness to drive:

  • potential impact of changing medications or dosage
  • cumulative effects of medications
  • presence of other medical conditions that may combine to adversely affect driving
  • other exacerbating factors (e.g. known history of alcohol or drug misuse).

Acute alcohol/drug intoxication is managed through specific road safety legislation (BAC limits, presence of certain drugs, drug impairment) — Appendix 4 (BAC limits), Appendix 5 (alcohol interlock programs). This is separate from long-term medical fitness/licensing; specific medical requirements not provided here. Chronic misuse/dependency of illicit, non-prescription and prescription drugs is a licensing issue — Part B section 9 Substance misuse.

General guidance for prescription drugs and driving. Most drugs (except benzodiazepines) don’t pose significantly increased crash risk once patient stabilised on treatment as prescribed. Considerations:

  • balance between potential impairment and improvement in health enabling safer driving
  • individual patient response variability
  • type of licence held and driving task nature (commercial assessments more stringent)
  • added risks of combining ≥2 impairing drugs, including alcohol
  • added risks of sleep deprivation/fatigue while driving (particularly commercial drivers)
  • potential impact of changing medications/dosage
  • cumulative effects of medications
  • presence of other conditions combining to adversely affect driving ability
  • other exacerbating factors (history of alcohol/drug misuse).

Effects of specific drug classes:

Medicinal cannabis (cannabinoids). Main active components: THC (psychoactive) and CBD. THC can cause cognitive/psychomotor impairments (attention/concentration deficits, mild cognitive impairment, dizziness, anxiety) beginning at low doses, highly individualised. Pharmacokinetics complex — severity of impairment hard to predict; influenced by history of use, dose, ratio of cannabinoids, route of administration (vaporised, oral, oral-mucosal, transdermal). Effects typically last 3–6 hours after inhalation or 5–8 hours after oral administration, but may be longer. CBD does not cause psychomotor/cognitive impairment or strong psychoactive effects at typical doses; may cause sedation/fatigue at higher doses and interact with other medications (may elevate plasma levels of some antiseizure drugs, some benzodiazepines).

Managing medicinal cannabis and driving: “start low, go slow” approach; administer at times unlikely to drive (e.g. at night before sleep). A period of restricted/non-driving, generally a minimum of four weeks, may be considered while adaptation to medication/treatment outcomes is determined. Alcohol should be avoided with medicinal cannabis due to additive effects/increased crash risk.

Assessing fitness to drive on medicinal cannabis: assess underlying chronic condition/disability per applicable standards; consider driving task, cognitive/visuospatial/motor impairment from condition or medication, and treatment outcomes. Conditions with specific standards (seizures — Part B 6.2; chronic pain — Part B 5) may be assessed under existing criteria; others per section 2 general guidance.

Medicinal cannabis and commercial licence holders: commercial standards more stringent, reflecting greater exposure/risk. Sleep deprivation/fatigue are common risks. Considerations: vehicle type, goods transported, distances/roads, cumulative driving time, night driving/sleep pattern disruption, dosage timing.

Medicinal cannabis and drug driving laws: drug driving/enforcement laws vary by state/territory. Generally illegal to drive with any THC present in bodily fluids (blood/saliva/urine), with no exceptions for therapeutic use in most jurisdictions. Tasmania provides a medical defence for driving with THC present if the medicinal cannabis is obtained/administered per the Poisons Act 1971 (Tas) — still illegal if impaired, and drivers must comply with roadside testing directions. Interstate travel/differing jurisdiction treatment should be discussed. CBD is not subject to drug driving controls provided treatment is free of impairing side effects/interactions.

Benzodiazepines. Well known to increase crash risk — found in about 4% of fatalities and 16% of injured drivers taken to hospital. If a hypnotic is needed, a shorter-acting drug is preferred. Tolerance to sedative effects of longer-acting benzodiazepines used for anxiety gradually reduces their adverse impact on driving skills.

Antidepressants. One of the more commonly detected drug groups in fatally injured drivers, reflecting wide community use. Greater impairment potential with sedating tricyclics (e.g. amitriptyline, dothiepin) than less-sedating SSRIs/SNRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline). Can reduce psychomotor/cognitive impairment caused by depression and improve driving performance by returning mood towards normal.

Antipsychotics. Diverse class; can improve performance if substantial psychotic-related cognitive deficits present. Most are sedating and can adversely affect driving via central dopaminergic and other receptor blockade. Older drugs (e.g. chlorpromazine) very sedating due to additional cholinergic/histamine actions. Newer drugs vary: clozapine, olanzapine, quetiapine — sedating; aripiprazole, risperidone, ziprasidone — less sedating. Sedation may be a particular problem early in treatment and at higher doses.

Opioids. CNS depressants that can suppress cognitive/psychomotor responses. Cognitive performance reduced early in treatment (mainly sedative effects); neuroadaptation rapidly established — patients on a stable dose may not have higher crash risk, including buprenorphine/methadone for dependency once dose stabilised for some weeks and not abusing other impairing substances. Night driving may be a problem due to persistent miotic effects reducing peripheral vision.

Further opiate-prescribing guidance: RACP Prescription Opioid Policy; ANZCA Faculty of Pain Medicine statement on opioid use in chronic non-cancer pain; RACGP Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice; local health agency websites.

2.3. Assessing and supporting functional driver capacity

2.3.1. Practical driver assessments. Impact of a condition/multiple conditions/disability on driving is not always clear, so a practical driver assessment may be useful. Different from entry-level competency tests; suitable only for persistent impairments.

When indicated: designed to assess impact of injury, illness, disability or ageing on driving skills including judgement, decision-making, observation, vehicle handling. May help determine need for special training in compensatory techniques or vehicle modification.

A health professional may request an assessment to supplement clinical assessment in borderline cases and assist recommendations. Limitations: condition may fluctuate (good/bad days); not possible to create emergency situations to assess reaction time. Assessments inform but do not necessarily override clinical opinion. Clearly unsuitable for on-road assessment: significant visual impairment or significant cognitive impairment.

Types of assessments available: off-road, on-road, driving simulator assessments — for cars, motorcycles, buses, heavy vehicles — conducted/overseen by occupational therapists trained in driver assessment or others approved by the DLA (e.g. training providers for commercial drivers). Processes vary between states/territories; initiated by examining health professional, other referrers (police, self, family) or the DLA.

What a practical assessment involves: usually two components — (a) off-road screening (evaluates nature/frequency/requirement for driving, underlying impairments, road law knowledge, insight, medical history, requirements for on-road test) and (b) in-car practical driver assessment (evaluates need for specialised equipment/vehicle modifications, ability to control the vehicle, functional status while driving — cognitive function, physical strength/skills, reaction time, insight, ability to self-monitor).

Recommendations may relate to licence status, vehicle modifications, rehabilitation/retraining, licence conditions/restrictions, and reassessment.

More information: VicRoads’ Guidelines for Occupational therapy driver assessors, 3rd edition, March 2018; Appendix 10 Specialist driver assessors; contact local DLA (Appendix 9).

2.3.2. Driver rehabilitation. A practical assessment may indicate need for a rehabilitation or retraining program, graded to increase difficulty/complexity; may include clinic-based activities, simulator/computer-based training, or on-road training with a driving instructor under an OT’s direction. May include training in vehicle modifications/aids and education to develop driver awareness/confidence. Limited evidence supports particular rehab/retraining strategies specifically, though simulation activities may offer controlled, repeatable conditions unavailable on-road. On completion, reassessment of driving skills and a report sent to the DLA with recommendations regarding competency/licensing.

2.3.3. Equal employment opportunity and discrimination. Purpose of standards (esp. commercial driving) is to protect public safety, not act as a barrier to employment per se. The conditional licence system supports employability without compromising road safety via periodic medical review and driving conditions. Commonwealth and state/territory legislation protects workers against unfair discrimination based on disability; if a patient suspects unfair discrimination based on the disability outlined on a conditional licence, they may contact their union, the Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission, or the relevant state/territory commission.

2.3.4. Information and assistance for drivers. Assessment by a health professional is one input into the DLA’s decision (which may cancel, refuse or suspend a licence, or place conditions on it). Because a licence is critical to independence/employment/recreation, withdrawal risk can evoke strong emotions (upset, anxious, frustrated, angry) — see 3.3.2 Patient–health professional relationship.

Where licensing decisions may affect a patient’s livelihood, the health professional should show sensitivity; timely medical reports are important; offering coping-strategy direction may help alleviate concerns. Where appropriate, direct referral rather than merely providing information sources:

  • Vocational assessors assess ability to rehabilitate, retrain, reskill for another industry/sector.
  • Government-funded assistance programs may support work-based assessments and workplace modifications including vehicle modifications.
  • Condition-specific support/advocacy agencies offer advice/support/services — e.g. Diabetes Australia, Dementia Australia, MS Australia, Epilepsy Action Australia, Epilepsy Foundation.

For older drivers, early advice helps plan for inevitable changes in independence. Some DLAs have dedicated fact sheets on impacts of ageing and common medical conditions on driving safety — check the licensing authority website in your state/territory.

3. Roles and responsibilities

The responsibility for issuing, renewing, suspending, refusing, cancelling or reinstating a person’s driver licence (including a conditional licence) lies ultimately with the driver licensing authority (DLA). Licensing decisions are based on a full consideration of relevant factors relating to the driver’s health and driving performance record.

Figure 2 relationships: Health professionals should advise patients if a medical condition, treatment or drink/drunk driving behaviours impact ability to drive safely, short or long term. Drivers are legally required to inform the DLA of serious illnesses affecting driving ability. The DLA may request drivers to have a medical examination. Health professionals and DLAs do not normally communicate directly (protects patient confidentiality) — however, with the driver’s consent, DLAs may communicate with health professionals when clarification/further information is needed; health professionals should consider reporting directly to the DLA when a patient continues driving despite appropriate advice and is likely to endanger the public.

Table 2. Key roles and responsibilities with respect to fitness to drive

Driver Health professional Driver licensing authority
Report to the DLA any long-term/permanent injury, illness, medical condition, disability or treatment that may affect ability to drive safely. Assess the person’s fitness to drive based on relevant clinical/functional information and relevant published medical standards. Make all decisions regarding licensing of drivers, considering reports from health professionals, police, members of the public, crash involvement and driving histories.
Respond truthfully to questions from a health professional about health status and likely impact on driving. Advise the person about: the impact of their condition/disability on ability to drive and recommend restrictions, ongoing monitoring, rehabilitation/training or transitional arrangements as required; their responsibility to report their condition to the DLA if it may affect safe driving. Make all decisions regarding issue of conditional licences, considering recommendations of health professionals and other relevant factors.
Adhere to prescribed medical treatment. Treat, monitor and manage the person’s condition with ongoing consideration of fitness to drive. Educate the driving public of their responsibility to report any long-term/permanent injury, illness, medical condition, disability or treatment that may affect ability to drive safely.
Comply with requirements of a conditional licence as appropriate, including periodic medical reviews. Report to the DLA regarding a person’s fitness to drive, including suitability for a conditional licence, in accordance with legislated requirements and public safety/ethical considerations. Provide relevant information resources and support for health professionals about driver fitness assessment and licensing.
For drivers who have previously advised the DLA about their health and driving, report any changes to their health that could affect ability to drive safely as soon as practicable (do not wait for periodic review). Note: medical practitioners or other clinicians do not have the legal authority to restrict, reinstate or apply conditions to a patient’s driver licence — this can only be done by the relevant DLA.

Brochures describing responsibilities of patients, health professionals and licensing authorities may be available from state/territory DLAs. Appendix 9 for contact details; also www.austroads.com.au.

3.1. Roles and responsibilities of driver licensing authorities

Responsibility for issuing, renewing, suspending, refusing or cancelling a licence (incl. conditional) lies ultimately with DLAs. Licensing decisions are individualised, based on:

  • health
  • functional capacity (including ability to compensate for any impairment)
  • insight into their condition
  • compliance with any prescribed treatment
  • compliance with existing licence conditions
  • driving history
  • any other relevant information.

The DLA seeks input directly from the driver and/or a health professional, and acts on unsolicited reports from health professionals, police or members of the public. Under national arrangements at time of publication, the DLA issuing the licence and the driver’s residential address should be in the same jurisdiction. Payment for health examinations/assessments is generally not the responsibility of DLAs. Each state/territory has an appeal system for licence decision disagreements; the DLA informs drivers of the appeal process.

DLAs can provide health professionals with information about: licensing/administrative processes; medical aspects (not all DLAs have medical officers on staff, but can assist with guidance); practical driver assessments; legal and ethical issues (general advice on legal/ethical issues → professional defence organisation). Appendix 9 has DLA contact details.

3.2. Roles and responsibilities of drivers

In all states/territories, legislation requires a driver to advise their DLA of any long-term/permanent injury/illness, disability or medical treatment that may affect safe driving ability. At licence application/renewal, drivers may be asked to complete a health declaration (e.g. diabetes, epilepsy, cardiovascular disease). Based on this, the DLA may request a medical examination. Drivers have a duty to declare health status and respond truthfully to any questions for this purpose.

Drivers must also report to the DLA when they become aware of a health condition that may affect safe driving ability. Reporting requirements vary between states/territories — drivers/health professionals should check local requirements; failure to report may carry penalties (Appendix 3 Legislation relating to reporting).

Drivers may be liable at common law if they continue driving knowing of a condition likely to adversely affect safe driving; failure to report can have long-term financial, insurance and legal consequences.

3.3.1. Confidentiality, privacy and reporting to the DLA. Health professionals have both an ethical and legal duty to maintain patient confidentiality. However, on rare occasions there are ethically/legally justifiable reasons for breaching confidentiality — the duty is legally qualified in certain circumstances to protect public safety. Health professionals should consider reporting directly to the DLA where a patient is either:

  • unable to appreciate the impact of their condition
  • unable to take notice of the health professional’s recommendations due to cognitive impairment
  • provides unreliable information on their condition, or
  • continues driving despite appropriate advice and is likely to endanger the public.

Jurisdictional variation: In the ACT, NSW, Qld, Tas, Vic and WA, statute provides that health professionals who report in good faith (without patient consent) that a patient is unfit to drive are protected from civil and criminal liability. The Northern Territory does not currently provide this protection. In SA and the NT, current legislation imposes mandatory reporting — a positive duty on health professionals to notify the relevant authority in writing of a belief that a driver is physically or mentally unfit to drive (Appendix 3).

It is preferable that action in the interests of public safety be taken with patient consent wherever possible, and with the patient’s knowledge. Failure to inform the patient exacerbates mistrust. An exception: where informing the patient may place the health professional or others at risk of violence (see 3.3.3).

Considerations when deciding to report directly to the DLA:

  • seriousness of the situation (immediate risks to public safety/others, from patient’s attitude and degree of risk)
  • risks associated with disclosure without consent/knowledge, balanced against implications of non-disclosure
  • the health professional’s ethical/professional obligations
  • whether circumstances indicate a serious and imminent threat to health, life or safety of any person.

Cases with an immediate threat to public safety may require reporting the driver to the DLA or police (e.g. history of reckless driving, crashes, or intentions to cause harm involving motor vehicles).

Examinations requested by a DLA: different confidentiality situation — patient presents with a form/letter requesting examination for licence application/renewal or conditional licence stipulation. Completed form should be sent directly to the DLA, not returned to the driver. Electronic medical report forms are returned directly to the DLA.

Privacy legislation: all health professionals and DLAs should be aware of National Privacy Principles, Health Privacy Principles and other applicable privacy legislation (e.g. health records legislation) when collecting/managing patient information and forwarding to third parties.

3.3.2. Patient–health professional relationship. Health professionals expected to act objectively assessing fitness to drive. If this cannot be achieved (e.g. possibility of the patient ceasing contact/avoiding medical management), the health professional should be prepared to disqualify themselves and refer the patient to another practitioner.

A difficult ethical situation arises when there is reason to doubt the veracity of information provided by a patient regarding health/capacity to drive safely. Strategies to consider:

  • contacting professional indemnity insurer, discussing the problem, documenting advice
  • discussing with colleagues
  • referring for a second/specialist opinion
  • contacting the relevant DLA and, without identifying the patient, discussing the problem and documenting the advice.

3.3.3. Patient hostility towards the health professional. Sometimes patients feel affronted by possible restriction/withdrawal of licence and may be hostile towards their treating health professional. The health professional may refer the driver to another practitioner or refer directly to the DLA without a fitness-to-drive recommendation. DLAs will not place pressure on health professionals that might needlessly expose them to risk of harassment or intimidation. May refer the patient to the standards themselves (developed by the NTC in cooperation with professional/allied health associations and road safety experts). More information on managing patient–professional hostility: RACGP website (racgp.org.au/your-practice/business/tools/safetyprivacy/gpsafeplace/).

3.3.4. Dealing with individuals who are not regular patients. Care needed — some drivers may seek to deceive health professionals about medical history/status, or “doctor shop” for a desirable opinion. If doubts exist about a person’s reason for seeking consultation, consider:

  • asking permission to request the person’s medical file from their regular health professional
  • conducting a more thorough examination than usual
  • noting on the medical report the length of time the patient has been known to the health professional and whether they had access to the full medical record/history.

3.3.5. Role of medical specialists. In most circumstances, GPs can conduct medical assessments of drivers of either commercial or private vehicles. However, if doubt exists about fitness to drive, or the condition/circumstances are not specifically covered by the standards, review by a specialist experienced in the condition is warranted; the GP should refer the patient. Treating specialists should share fitness-to-drive assessment outcomes with the patient’s GP for coordination of care/monitoring.

For commercial vehicle drivers, the opinion of a medical specialist is generally required for initial recommendation and periodic review of a conditional licence — main exceptions set out in 4.4.7. This reflects the higher safety risk and importance of expert opinion for commercial drivers. Where specialist access is limited, alternative arrangements for subsequent reviews by the GP may be made with DLA approval and agreement of the specialist and treating GP.

Note: the opinion of a specialist is relevant only to their specialty. GPs are well placed to integrate reports from various specialists for multiple disabilities. An occupational physician or authorised health professional may provide a similar role for commercial drivers and their employers. “Specialist” in this publication = a medical/surgical specialist other than a GP (Fellows of the RACGP and Fellows of the Australian College of Rural and Remote Medicine have specialist status under current medical registration arrangements — www.medicalboard.gov.au).

Box 2. Telehealth. GPs and patients are encouraged to use telemedicine (e.g. videoconferencing) to minimise difficulties seeing their regular GP or where specialist access is limited. From 30 March 2020, telehealth (video-call) and phone consultation items became available to all Medicare-eligible Australians for a wide range of consultations, subject to certain limitations — particularly helpful for remote communities. Introduced in response to COVID-19; a longer-term telehealth model (post 31 December 2021) was under development at time of writing. More info: humanservices.gov.au/health-professionals/services/medicare/mbs-and-telehealth.

3.3.6. Role of driver assessors and trainers. A practical driver assessment (on/off-road) may be required to assess impact of injury, illness, disability or ageing on driving skills (judgement, decision-making, observation, vehicle handling) — particularly useful in borderline cases involving vehicle modifications/adaptations or where impact on functionality is unclear. Should be conducted by suitably qualified occupational therapy driving assessors. Availability/access advice from the local DLA and Occupational Therapy Australia (Appendix 10 Specialist driver assessors). Recommendations may relate to licence status, need for vehicle modifications, rehabilitation/retraining (2.3.2), licence conditions/restrictions (4.4), and reassessment. Driver training and rehabilitation providers support drivers to retain/regain skills after injury/disability/illness and to adapt to vehicle modifications; training may be on-road and supplemented by simulator/computer-based training.

3.3.7. Role of independent experts/panels. Not all medical and driving circumstances can be specifically or fully covered in these standards — DLAs may draw on independent expert medical advice to inform borderline or otherwise difficult licensing decisions.

3.3.8. Documentation. Clear documentation of assessment results and communication with the patient and DLA is important (see 5.2 Which forms to use).

4. Licensing and medical fitness to drive

4.1. Medical standards for private and commercial vehicle drivers

Two standards outlined: private vehicle driver standards and commercial vehicle driver standards. Assignment of standards is based on an evaluation of driver, passenger and public safety risk, where:

Risk = Likelihood of the event × Severity of consequences.

Commercial vehicle crashes may present a severe threat to passengers, other road users (including pedestrians/cyclists) and residents adjacent to the road — potential for chemical spillage, fire, significant property damage. Private vehicle crashes are likely to have less severe consequences.

Commercial vehicle drivers generally spend considerable time on the road (increasing crash likelihood) and may also be monitoring in-vehicle communication/work-related systems — a further factor increasing crash likelihood. Crash data: commercial vehicle drivers are more than twice as likely to be involved in a fatal crash compared with other drivers. To ensure risk to the public is similar for private and commercial drivers, medical fitness requirements for commercial standards must be more stringent.

Identifying which standards apply: guided by both the type of vehicle (e.g. heavy vehicle) and the purpose for which the driver is authorised (e.g. carrying passengers or dangerous goods). Generally, commercial standards apply to drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles, or vehicles carrying dangerous goods. A dangerous goods driver licence is required to transport dangerous goods in an individual receptacle with capacity greater than 500 litres or net mass greater than 500 kilograms.

Private standards should be applied to:

  • drivers applying for/holding licence class C (car), R (motorcycle) or LR (light rigid), unless also applying for authority to carry public passengers for hire/reward or dangerous goods, or (in some jurisdictions) for a driving instructor
  • voluntary drivers using their private vehicle for a voluntary service (e.g. meals on wheels, school staff driving students, voluntary taxi services for older people, L2P drivers), unless the voluntary driving aligns with commercial standards.

Commercial standards should be applied to:

  • drivers of “heavy vehicles” — holding/applying for licence class MR (medium rigid), HR (heavy rigid), HC (heavy combination) or MC (multiple combination)
  • drivers carrying public passengers for hire or reward (bus drivers, taxi/rideshare drivers, chauffeurs, hire cars and small buses)
  • drivers carrying dangerous goods
  • drivers subject to Basic or Advanced Fatigue Management requirements under the National Heavy Vehicle Accreditation Standard
  • other driver categories subject to commercial standards due to certification/industry standard requirements (e.g. driving instructors, members of TruckSafe).

4.2. Considerations for commercial vehicle licensing

Commercial standards acknowledge/allow for variability of risk among different commercial drivers. The DLA considers the nature of the driving task as well as the medical condition, particularly for conditional licences. E.g., a farmer needing a commercial licence for occasional heavy vehicle use on their own property differs from an interstate multiple-combination vehicle driver.

Approaches adopted to manage increased risk of commercial driving (Table 3):

  • generally longer non-driving periods prescribed for commercial vehicle drivers vs private (e.g. after a seizure or heart attack)
  • generally a requirement that a specialist (rather than GP) provides information for a commercial conditional licence
  • some medical conditions may preclude commercial driving but still allow a full or conditional private licence (e.g. early dementia)
  • the review period for a conditional licence may be shorter for a commercial driver.

Table 3. Choice of standard according to vehicle/licence type

National licence class Description Applicable standard
Motorcycle (R) Motorbike or motortrike Private standards apply unless the driver holds/applies for authority to carry public passengers for hire/reward → commercial standards apply.
Car (C) Vehicle not more than 4.5 tonnes GVM, seating up to 12 adults incl. driver Private standards apply unless the driver: holds/applies for authority to carry public passengers for hire/reward (e.g. taxi driver); is undertaking medical assessment as an accreditation scheme requirement; holds/applies for a dangerous goods driver licence; holds/applies for authority to be a driving instructor (varies by jurisdiction) → in these cases, commercial standards apply.
Light rigid (LR) Rigid vehicle >4.5 t GVM, or seating >12 adults, ≤8 tonnes, plus trailer ≤9 t GVM As above.
Medium rigid (MR) Two-axle rigid vehicle >8 t GVM, plus trailer ≤9 t GVM Commercial standards apply at all times.
Heavy rigid (HR) Rigid vehicle with ≥3 axles >8 t GVM, plus trailer ≤9 t GVM Commercial standards apply at all times.
Heavy combination (HC) Prime mover + single semitrailer >9 t GVM and any unladen converter dolly trailer Commercial standards apply at all times.
Multiple combination (MC) Heavy combination vehicle with more than one trailer Commercial standards apply at all times.

Notes on national licence classes and standards:

  • A person not meeting commercial vehicle medical requirements may still be eligible to retain a private licence — both sets of standards may need to be consulted.
  • DLA periodic/medical examination requirements for each licence class are outlined in Appendix 1.
  • Standards intended for drivers within the ambit of ordinary road laws. Special-exemption drivers (emergency service and first responder vehicle drivers) should have a risk assessment and appropriate medical standard applied by the employer — due to nature of work (carrying patients unrestrained on stretchers/in locked vans, working shifts, under pressure), at minimum should be considered under the commercial driver standard.

4.3. Prescribed periodic medical examinations for particular licensing/authorisation classes

Some driver classes must present periodically for prescribed examinations per licensing/authorisation requirements. Requirements vary between states/territories, may apply to:

  • drivers of vehicles physically difficult to drive or requiring capacity to monitor many vehicle functions (e.g. multiple combinations)
  • drivers of vehicles where crash consequences are usually serious (e.g. dangerous goods licence holders, public passenger vehicle drivers).

Some states/territories also require periodic medical assessment for older drivers beyond a specified age. Determined/directed by individual state/territory DLAs; outlined in Appendix 1. Industry groups (Australian Trucking Association) and national programs (Fatigue Management Program under National Heavy Vehicle Accreditation Standard) may also require periodic examinations (not discussed specifically in this standard).

4.4. Conditional licences

4.4.1. What is a conditional licence? A mechanism for optimising driver and public safety while maintaining driver independence when a driver has a long-term or progressive health condition or injury that may affect safe driving. Permits driving under conditions suited to capability — e.g. no night driving, driving only in familiar areas (local area restriction), wearing corrective lenses. Identifies need for medical treatments, vehicle modifications or driving restrictions. May specify a review period, after which the person must undertake a medical review to establish continued fitness to drive. Offers an alternative to licence withdrawal and enables individual case-based decision making.

4.4.2. Who allocates a conditional licence? Final decision rests with the DLA, based on information from the driver’s health professional and on-road safety considerations. The DLA issues a conditional licence on the basis that any additional road safety risk posed is acceptable.

4.4.3. Role of the health professional. The health professional advises the DLA of:

  • which medical requirements (for an unconditional licence) have not been met (referencing medical criteria/thresholds in this document)
  • likely adequacy of treatments, driver aides or vehicle modifications in optimising driver capacity
  • the plan to monitor the driver’s performance and medical condition, including timeframes for review
  • if appropriate, information relating to possible licence conditions (vehicle type, licence restrictions e.g. no night driving, radius restriction, downgrading to a lower class of licence)
  • any other medical information relevant to the driving task.

4.4.4. What sort of conditions/restrictions may be recommended? Examples (Table 4) are indicative only, vary by condition and licence type. Include standard conditions appearing as codes on the driver licence (corrective lenses, automatic transmission, hand controls) and advisory conditions which may not appear on the licence (e.g. take medication as prescribed, don’t drive more than a specified number of hours in any 24-hour period).

One option to maintain independence: a local area (radius) restriction based on home address — limits where the person can drive; only suitable for drivers who can reliably remember the limits and compensate for functional decline, and respond appropriately/timely to unexpected occurrences (roadworks, detours). Individuals lacking insight or with significant visual, memory or cognitive-perceptual impairments are usually not suitable candidates for a radius restriction (e.g. Part B 6.1 Dementia).

Table 4. Examples of licence conditions that may be required by the DLA (not mandatory requirements; may be unsuitable in some circumstances)

Example of disability/situation Example of licence condition
Left leg disability Automatic transmission
Left arm disability Automatic transmission, steering aide
Short stature Built-up seat and pedals
Loss of bilateral leg function Hand-operated acceleration/brake controls
Reduced lower limb strength Power brakes required
Reduced upper limb strength Power steering required; steering aide
Short leg(s) Extended pedals
Hearing deficiency (commercial drivers) Hearing aid must be worn (assuming hearing standard met)
Deafness, both ears (commercial driver, assuming hearing standard met) Vehicle fitted with two external rear-view mirrors and other devices to assist external visual surveillance/recognition of emergency vehicles (e.g. wide-angle internal mirror, rear-view camera)
Visual acuity deficiency Prescribed corrective lenses must be worn
Loss of limb function Prosthesis must be worn
Degenerative medical conditions Periodic review by driver assessor
Night blindness Driving in daylight hours only
Age or medical condition-associated impairments, e.g. attention Driving during off-peak only; within a specified km radius of home; daylight hours only; no freeway driving (local area restriction)
Spinal cord injury (above T12) Not to drive when temperature is above 25°C unless the vehicle is air-conditioned
Substance misuse (alcohol) Ignition interlock device

4.4.5. What monitoring is required for a conditional licence? Conditional licences should be subject to periodic review to monitor the medical condition, disability or treatment, including compliance. Frequency of formal review is sometimes specified in this publication but often left to the judgement of the health professional given variations in severity/stability and possible driving effects. The health professional should advise the DLA of the period for which a conditional licence could be issued before formal review (months to years depending on the condition/progression); these reviews differ from ordinary follow-up consultations offered during general management.

If, at a periodic review or during general management, the patient no longer meets the conditional licence requirements (health deteriorated), the patient should be advised to inform the DLA of changed circumstances (3.2).

4.4.6. Conditional licences for commercial vehicle drivers. DLA may consider a conditional commercial licence, e.g. in circumstances where crash risk exposure can be managed. A case-by-case risk assessment is required considering relevant factors: driver insight, stability of the health condition, treatment compliance, nature of goods transported, size/complexity of the vehicle, periodic review requirements. Examples of circumstances: off-road driving of commercial vehicles where licences are still required; where driving is not the primary occupation (mechanics test-driving vehicles, primary producers who need product to market a couple of times a year, drivers who need to move buses not carrying public passengers within a bus depot or nearby workshop).

For commercial vehicle drivers, the opinion of a medical specialist is generally required for consideration of a conditional licence — main exceptions in 4.4.7. This reflects the higher safety risk and importance of expert opinion. Where specialist access is difficult, the DLA may agree to a process where: initial assessment/advice is provided by a specialist; ongoing periodic review for the conditional licence is provided by the treating GP in cooperation with the specialist. Telemedicine is encouraged to facilitate specialist access where appropriate.

4.4.7. What if there is a delay before a specialist can be seen? For a commercial vehicle driver or applicant assessed by a GP as not meeting criteria for an unconditional licence for one or more conditions, but who may meet criteria for a conditional licence, the DLA may permit the person to drive/continue driving a commercial vehicle pending assessment by an appropriate specialist(s) if:

  • the person has an appointment to see the relevant specialist(s) at the earliest practicable opportunity, and
  • in the GP’s opinion, the condition(s) are not likely to lead to acute incapacity or loss of cognitive ability or insight before the assessment occurs.

Examples of conditions suitable for this interim arrangement: early peripheral neuropathy, early rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes treated by diet and exercise alone. Examples of conditions that could lead to acute incapacity or loss of concentration (not suitable): ischaemic heart disease, sleep apnoea, blackouts (other than vasovagal). The DLA may impose conditions on the licence in applying this section.

4.5. Reinstatement of licences or removal or variation of licence conditions

Situations may arise where a medical condition improves such that the patient’s licence restriction may be reconsidered by the DLA, resulting in reinstatement of the licence or removal/variation of licence conditions, including periodic medical review requirements.

A letter or notification to this effect from the treating health professional to the DLA (refer Appendix 2.2 Medical condition notification form) should include:

  • details of the requirements now met which were not previously met (refer to medical criteria in this document)
  • the response to treatment, interventions and/or rehabilitation, and the long-term prognosis
  • the duration of improvement
  • other relevant information, including consideration of the driving task (e.g. requirements of a person who drives occasionally to the shops are likely to differ from those undertaking extensive interstate travel or regular employment/voluntary-work driving).

The DLA will consider the request and advise the driver of their determination; licence decisions may be contingent on the driver/applicant undertaking and passing an on-road evaluation to confirm driving abilities.

5. Assessment and reporting process — step by step

Assessing fitness to drive is based on the decision-making process outlined below. The nature/extent of examination depends on the circumstances and reasons for examination.

Figure 3. Medical decision-making process for assessing fitness to drive (summary)

  • Temporary condition affecting driving ability in the short term (examples: mydriatics, general anaesthetic, fractures) → Not fit to drive in short term: advise patient of appropriate temporary driving restrictions; if not a licensing issue, no report to DLA required; may be a fitness-for-duty issue for commercial drivers — advise driver to notify their employer.
  • Long-term condition or disability (examples: diabetes, cardiac, neurological, psychiatric, congenital, acquired brain injury, cognitive impairment) → refer to requirements for licensing → Are requirements for an unconditional licence met?
    • Yes → Fit to drive (with no restrictions).
    • No → Are requirements for a conditional licence met?
      • Yes → Fit to drive with restrictions/conditions on licence — advise patient of legal requirement to notify DLA; advise/notify DLA directly as appropriate.
      • No → Not fit to drive — advise patient of legal requirement to notify DLA; advise/notify DLA directly as appropriate.
      • Not sure → Unsure of fitness to drive — refer to appropriate specialist and/or refer for practical driver assessment (2.3.1) and/or refer to DLA.

5.1. Steps in the assessment and reporting process

Step 1: Consider the type of licence held or applied for. The type of licence determines whether commercial or private medical standards apply. For DLA-requested examinations, the DLA identifies the licence type on the request. For assessment within an ongoing therapeutic relationship, the health professional determines from the patient what licence/authority they hold — patients may withhold information if mobility/livelihood is threatened, so health professionals should routinely be aware of patients’ occupations. Refer to Table 3 to determine which standards to apply. Commercial standards are more stringent than private; a person ineligible for a commercial licence may still be eligible for a private licence — both sets of standards may need consulting.

Step 2: Establish relevant medical and driving history. Nature/extent varies by circumstance. For a first-time DLA-requested examination, a detailed history should establish:

  • whether the person has ever been found unfit to drive in the past, and the reasons
  • history of epilepsy, syncope or other conditions of impaired consciousness, including: sleep disorders; neurological conditions; psychiatric conditions; problems from alcohol and/or drugs; diabetes; cardiovascular conditions (especially ischaemic heart disease); locomotor disorders; hearing or visual problems
  • history of motor vehicle incidents (crashes, near misses, driving offences, drink/drug driving)
  • whether the person is taking medications that might affect driving ability
  • existence of other medical conditions that, combined, might exacerbate road safety risks (2.2.8 Multiple medical conditions)
  • degree of insight the patient has into their ability to drive safely
  • nature of current driving patterns and needs — how frequently, for what purposes, over what distances, and whether they travel at night.

Special “for cause” examinations may be requested by the DLA out of concern for driving behaviour (e.g. recurrent crashes) — desirable that all aspects of the driver–vehicle–road system be considered (Figure 1), e.g. fatigue factors for commercial drivers. A full medical history and history of any crashes should be taken and a complete physical examination conducted.

For conditional licence review requested by the DLA, history is likely well established; focus on recent status of the particular condition(s) and impacts on driving/general functionality. For assessment during ongoing therapeutic relationship, medical history likely well established; may need exploration of driving history.

Step 3: Undertake a clinical examination. For DLA-requested examinations, a comprehensive clinical examination generally required — assessing functionality of body systems including physical and cognitive functioning. Focus on determining risk of involvement in a serious crash caused by inability to control the vehicle or inability to act/react appropriately. This publication focuses on common conditions affecting fitness to drive long-term (Part B), but it is not possible to define all clinical situations that would compromise public safety — unusual conditions, systemic disorders, or several co-occurring conditions may have additive/cumulative detrimental effects on judgement and overall function (2.2.8). Additional tests or specialist referral may be required if clinical examination raises the possibility of potentially significant problems.

Step 4: Consider the clinical examination results in conjunction with the patient’s medical history, driving history and driving needs. Upon consideration of available information, the health professional may draw one of the following conclusions:

  1. The person has a temporary condition that may affect their driving ability in the short term but will not affect their licence status.
  2. The person complies with all medical requirements appropriate to the type of licence held or requested.
  3. The person does not meet the unconditional licensing requirements, but medical treatments and/or vehicle or driving modifications may enable them to drive safely under a conditional licence.
  4. The person does not meet the medical requirements for an unconditional or conditional licence (not fit to drive).
  5. The health professional is in doubt about the patient’s fitness to drive.

Where doubt exists, or circumstances are not precisely covered by the standards, review by a specialist experienced in the particular condition is warranted. Where the specialist is also uncertain, a practical driver assessment (2.3.1) is one option. Clearance from the DLA may be required before an assessment takes place. Ultimately the case may need referral to the DLA for evaluation.

Note: the DLA is ultimately responsible by law for the licensing decision. It is sufficient for a health professional in such circumstances to prepare a report for the DLA stating the facts and their opinions clearly.

Where a condition of significance to driving is suspected but not proven (e.g. angina), the health professional should investigate; where doubt exists about safety of continued driving during investigation, the patient should be advised accordingly (2.2.4 Undifferentiated conditions).

Step 5: Inform and advise the patient. Health professionals should routinely advise patients how their condition may impair ability to drive safely — informing the patient about the nature of their condition, extent of control over it, importance of periodic medical review, and need for regular medication where appropriate. For temporary conditions affecting driving short-term, advise about not driving and, with patient consent, seek support from family members as required; notification to the DLA is not required in such instances.

For DLA-requested examinations, the advisory process is straightforward — the patient is actively seeking an examination as part of licence application/renewal or a conditional licence requirement, and will return the report to the DLA. If found not to meet medical criteria, the health professional should take a conciliatory and supportive role, fully explaining the risks posed, being particularly aware of livelihood implications; special considerations apply for individuals who are not regular patients (3.3.4).

The situation may be more challenging when fitness to drive is considered in the course of a patient’s regular treatment and they are found not to meet the medical criteria — the patient may perceive the health professional as making the licensing decision (though they are not). Where the health professional believes continued driving/unconditional driving would likely be dangerous, the patient should be informed of the risk to themselves and others; involving a family member/friend where possible is helpful. The driver should be encouraged to report their condition voluntarily to the DLA and reminded of their legal obligation to do so. The standards in this publication should be consulted, since they carry authority not imposed by the individual health professional but by national consensus of DLAs.

Information brochures may be available from the DLA to support the patient advisory process (Appendix 9); a range of driver information resources are listed in 2.3.4. Where patients are found not to meet medical criteria or conditions/restrictions are recommended, advice regarding alternative means of transport should be provided, including reference to disabled car parking and taxi services (Appendix 6).

Step 6: Report to the driver licensing authority as appropriate. For a DLA-requested examination, the reporting process involves completing the relevant form provided by the DLA via the patient. Only information relevant to the patient’s ability to drive should be included in the report, and it should be signed by the examining professional. The original medical report should go to the patient to return to the DLA; a copy kept on file in the patient’s medical record. Since the patient generally returns the report, signed consent is not usually needed for this; however, the DLA may ask the patient for signed consent for the DLA to contact the health professional for additional information. Some states/territories provide an online medical report for completion by health professionals.

For assessments made during patient treatment, when encouraging patients to self-report their condition to the DLA, the health professional should complete a copy of the Medical condition notification form (Appendix 2.2) and provide it to the patient to take to the DLA. Some states/territories may provide an online version. It is recommended the health professional keep a copy of the Medical condition notification form in the patient record. The DLA will also accept a letter describing the patient’s condition and nature of any driving restrictions recommended.
